title: Bubble sort
starter: You have seven cards in a random order. Describe, precisely, how you would put them in order using only swaps between neighbours.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: One comparison
facts: If they are in the wrong order, swap them.
Move along one and compare the next pair.
stations.challenge: Describe what happens to one pair of items in a bubble sort.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Compare the first two items.
Also credit: If they are in the wrong order, swap them.

questions.q: In a bubble sort, which items are compared?
questions.a: Two items next to each other

questions.q: When does a bubble sort swap two items?
questions.a: When they are in the wrong order for the sort

stations.name: One pass
facts: A pass goes from one end of the list to the other, comparing every neighbouring pair.
After one pass the largest value has moved all the way to the end.
That is why it is called a bubble sort: values bubble up to their place.
stations.challenge: Carry out one pass on 5, 2, 9, 1 and write the result.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A pass goes from one end of the list to the other, comparing every neighbouring pair.
Also credit: After one pass the largest value has moved all the way to the end.

questions.q: Complete one pass of a bubble sort on this list. Tap two items to swap them.
What is guaranteed after one complete pass?
questions.a: The largest value is in its final position at the end

stations.name: Repeating the passes
facts: After each pass, one more value is in its final place.
The algorithm repeats until a pass makes no swaps at all.
A list of n items needs up to n minus 1 passes.
stations.challenge: How many passes would 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 need? Explain why.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: After each pass, one more value is in its final place.
Also credit: The algorithm repeats until a pass makes no swaps at all.

questions.q: How does a bubble sort know it has finished?
questions.a: A whole pass happens with no swaps

questions.q: A list of 6 items is in exactly reverse order. How many passes are needed?

stations.name: Why it is slow
facts: Each pass makes almost as many comparisons as there are items.
There can be almost as many passes as items, so the work grows with the square of the list size.
Doubling the list roughly quadruples the work.
stations.challenge: Explain why a bubble sort is unsuitable for a list of 100,000 items.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Each pass makes almost as many comparisons as there are items.
Also credit: There can be almost as many passes as items, so the work grows with the square of the list size.

questions.q: A list doubles in size. Roughly what happens to the work a bubble sort does?
Why is a bubble sort still taught?
questions.a: It is the easiest sorting algorithm to understand and to program

stations.name: Its advantages
facts: It is very simple to write, so it is hard to get wrong.
It sorts in place: it needs no second copy of the list.
On a nearly sorted list it finishes quickly, because the first pass makes almost no swaps.
stations.challenge: Give two situations where a bubble sort is an acceptable choice.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: It is very simple to write, so it is hard to get wrong.
Also credit: It sorts in place: it needs no second copy of the list.

questions.q: Which are genuine advantages of a bubble sort? Select all that apply.
questions.a: It is simple to program; It needs no extra copy of the list; It finishes quickly on a nearly sorted list; It is easy to explain
It rearranges the original list without needing a second copy

stations.name: Answering bubble sort questions
facts: Show the list after each pass, not after each swap, unless asked otherwise.
Say which items are being compared.
State the stopping condition: a pass with no swaps.
stations.challenge: Show every pass of a bubble sort on 4, 1, 3, 2.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Show the list after each pass, not after each swap, unless asked otherwise.
Also credit: Say which items are being compared.

questions.q: Complete one pass of a bubble sort on this list.
A question asks you to show the list after the first pass of a bubble sort on 9, 5, 7. What is the answer?

final.name: Final challenge: bubble it

questions.q: Complete one pass of a bubble sort on this list.
Is each statement true of a bubble sort?
questions.a: It compares items that are next to each other = True; It sorts the list in place = True; It stops when a pass makes no swaps = True; It requires the list to be sorted first = False; It is the fastest sorting algorithm = False; It splits the list in half = False

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe how a bubble sort works.
points: That is why it is called a bubble sort: values bubble up to their place.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: Show the contents of the list 5, 2, 9, 1 after the first pass of a bubble sort.
points: After one pass the largest value has moved all the way to the end.
That is why it is called a bubble sort: values bubble up to their place.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using a bubble sort.
points: That is why it is called a bubble sort: values bubble up to their place.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
